narrative.text: 02:10. The residence telephone rings twice and stops. Vyktor does not ring twice unless he wants you awake before you answer.
Central District. A student march on Corvin Bridge. Forty-two detained. One gave his name as Tomas Mikhaelson.
The desk sergeant knew the face anyway. He has put him on a separate sheet. Awaiting instruction.
The march was against the Bench removals. The placards say SIX JUDGES in red house paint. Tomas painted three of them on the floor of a flat in Corvin Street.
The march was against the Article 12 override. The placards say THE COURT IS NOT YOURS. Someone has underlined YOURS twice.
The march was about the student stipend, frozen since the spring at ₭31 a month. The placards are hand-lettered. Some of the spelling is wrong.

The station smells of wet wool and floor polish. Forty-one young people sit on the charge-room benches with their shoelaces in a cardboard box. Tomas is not among them. He is in the inspector's office, alone, with a cup of tea he has not touched.

Chancellor. I came when I heard. For the record: my officers drew no batons tonight. Sergeant Bek has done what sergeants do. He made a second sheet. I would like to know whether this government keeps second sheets.
I wrote a paper on this in 1958. 'The Second Ledger: Discretion as the Shadow of Law.' I never expected to stand in it. The sergeant is waiting for me to tell him what you want. I am waiting for you.
Chancellor. Nothing has been written down that cannot be unwritten. Bek is a sensible man. Twenty-two years. He knows how these nights go.
The duty inspector is a tired man with a ledger and nothing to say. He turns the second sheet around on the counter so you can read it.
Forty-one names on one sheet. One on the other. Father's name was on a sheet once. Somebody decided which pile.

choices.text: Go into the inspector's office. Close the door.

narrative.text: He stands when you come in. He is taller than he was in the spring. There is a cut over his left eyebrow that someone has cleaned badly.
They gave me tea. Nobody else got tea. Do you understand? Nobody out there got tea.
The steward's armband is still on his sleeve. The arrest report says he kept the march off the tram lines. It also says he would not leave when ordered.
Krel's file on him is still in the second drawer of my desk. I never read the last page. I wonder whether it says this.
Mikhaelson. I thought if I used his name they'd treat me like him. Instead they brought me tea. Don't fix this, Mama. Whatever you're about to do, don't make me a favor.
He says favor the way his grandfather would have said it. As an accusation.

choices.text: "Put him on the first sheet." Same bench, same magistrate, same fine as the other forty-one.
Tear up the second sheet. He leaves by the service door before the shift changes.
Release all forty-two. No charges. It was a march, not a riot.

narrative.text: Sergeant Bek reads the second sheet, looks at you once, and copies one name onto the first in the same blue ink as the others. Forty-two.

The magistrate sits at nine. Forty-two fines of ₭20. Tomas pays his own from a canvas wallet. The Veltrian Voice runs the docket on page three. The Herald runs it on page one: CHANCELLOR'S SON IN THE DOCK.
He leaves a note on the kitchen table that night. Three words, in pencil. Same bench. Thanks.
Twenty kroner and a front page. Cheap, as these things go. Vyktor says the Herald will cost a point in the polls. He says it like a man reading a receipt he has already paid.

choices.text: One ink, forty-two names. The Herald gets its front page.

narrative.text: Sergeant Bek folds the second sheet twice and puts it in his breast pocket, not the bin. You notice. He notices you noticing.
Tomas goes out through the service door at 03:15. Forty-one people on the benches watch the door open and close. One of them is the girl who carried his placard.
He does not come home. He sleeps on a friend's floor in Corvin Street for six nights. On the seventh he comes for his books and does not look at you.
Three fifteen. Thirty-two minutes before three forty-seven. I didn't pick the hour. I keep doing the arithmetic anyway.

choices.text: He walked free. Bek kept the sheet. Both will matter later.

narrative.text: Forty-two releases over the Chancellor's signature. My officers will read it one way: march anywhere you like, the Palace will sign. I'll need a month to undo that.
Good. Now do it on a night when your son isn't in the building. That is the version I will believe.
As you wish. Bek will remember this longer than the students will, Chancellor. So will the men who arrested them.
The students walk out onto Corvin Bridge at 03:40, singing something off-key. Tomas walks out last. He stops beside you at the door.
You did it for me. You know that. If I wasn't in there, they'd still be on the benches.
He is right. The forty-one are free anyway. Both things are true, and I don't get to choose which one he keeps.

choices.text: Forty-two free, and one son who knows exactly why.
